title: Know That I Am God
author: Anonymous / Multiple possible authors (specify if you have a particular author in mind)
publication_date: Varies (phrase appears in religious scripture; popularized in various spiritual works)
genre: Christianity (primarily, based on the phrase's origin)
target_audience: Individuals on a spiritual journey or exploration
Anyone interested in contemplative or meditative practices
core_themes: Letting go of control and surrendering to a higher power
The practice of stillness, meditation, and faith
Trust in God's sovereignty and plans
primary_purpose: To encourage readers to embrace faith, release anxiety, and recognize the presence and supremacy of God in all circumstances. The phrase invites reflection, surrender, and reconnection with the divine, often serving as a prompt for meditation or prayer.

structure_format.narrative_style: Reflective, meditative, and direct (when presented in scriptural or devotional settings); sometimes expanded upon in modern devotional literature with stories, reflections, prayers, and exercises
structure_format.organization: Often presented as a single verse, but topic can be expanded into chapters or essays reflecting on its meaning. Modern books may be divided into themed meditations or short daily devotionals.

key_concepts_lessons: Stillness and contemplation are vital for spiritual growth.
Recognizing God’s omnipotence can bring comfort and reduce anxiety.
Faith often involves letting go of one's own striving or control.
The world can be chaotic, but spiritual anchoring brings peace.
Active trust in God transforms one's perspective on challenges.
notable_features: Rooted in the biblical phrase 'Be still, and know that I am God' (Psalm 46:10)
Appears in sermons, devotionals, meditation guides, and inspirational books
Encourages personal application through contemplation or daily reflection
Frequently referenced in Christian and interfaith spiritual literature
cultural_historical_context: Originating from Psalm 46:10 in the Hebrew Bible/Old Testament, the phrase has resonated through centuries as an anchor for faith amidst turmoil. It is widely quoted in liturgy, devotional literature, meditative practices, and has found cross-denominational and even interfaith appeal in times of crisis or uncertainty.
reception_impact: Serves as a touchstone for Christian worship, counseling, and spiritual formation
Quoted in countless sermons, hymns, books, and inspirational media
Has been adapted widely in contemporary Christian literature and spiritual wellness circles
Praised for its universal message of peace, surrender, and faith; sometimes critiqued for being used as a simplistic answer to complex life situations
